title: Pull one file back from three commits ago
summary: A config file was right two weeks ago and wrong now. Get that one file back without reverting the commits around it, and learn to read any file from any point in history.
mental_model: `<commit>:<path>` names the content of a file inside a commit. Once you can write that, you can read it, diff it, or drop it into your working tree — no checkout, no branch switching, no time travel for the whole repo.

commit.message: Widen thresholds while debugging the alerting pipeline

steps.title: Find when the file last changed
steps.why: `log -- <path>` limits history to commits touching that file. Three commits of noise disappear and the culprit is obvious.

steps.title: See what that commit did to it
steps.why: Scoping a diff to one path is how you read a large commit. Here it shows debugging values that were never meant to survive.

steps.title: Read the old version without changing anything
steps.why: `git show <rev>:<path>` prints a file exactly as it was in that commit. Nothing on disk changes — this is the safest way to check a value before deciding what to do.
steps.expect: The sane thresholds, printed straight from history.

steps.title: Compare then and now
steps.why: Naming two revisions with a path shows just that file's drift. This is the diff you paste into the incident channel.

steps.title: Restore just that file
steps.why: `restore --source` writes the old content into your working tree, leaving every other file at its current state. The three commits around it are untouched — no revert, no reset.

verify.label: the old thresholds are back in the working tree

steps.title: Commit the correction with a message that explains it
steps.why: The commit records a deliberate reversal of one file. Anyone reading history later sees what happened and why, which a silent overwrite would not tell them.
commands: git commit -m "Restore production alert thresholds (debug values leaked in)"

steps.title: Revision syntax worth memorising
steps.why: `HEAD~2` is two first-parents back. `HEAD^2` is the second parent of a merge. `main@{1}` is where main pointed one move ago. Most 'how do I name that commit' questions end here.

verify.label: the sane thresholds are restored
verify.hint: git restore --source=HEAD~2 thresholds.yaml (before you committed the fix, HEAD~2 was the good one)

verify.label: app.py was left alone — you restored one file, not the whole tree
verify.hint: a git revert or reset would have dragged app.py back too

verify.label: the correction is a new commit on top, not a rewrite
verify.hint: commit the restored file rather than amending or resetting

pitfalls: `git checkout HEAD~2 -- <file>` is the older spelling and also stages the file. `restore --source` only touches the working tree unless you add `--staged`.
`git restore --source=<commit> .` restores the whole tree but leaves the branch where it is — an easy way to create a confusing 'revert everything' commit.
`HEAD~2` moves relative to where HEAD is *now*. After you commit the fix, the same expression names a different commit.
Reading a file with `git show <rev>:<path>` needs the path from the repository root, not relative to your current directory.
